screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you’ll learn how to measure Redis performance in a systematic way and then use that data to tune the system for real workloads. Benchmarking is the controlled act of generating load and observing throughput and latency. You will see concrete redis-benchmark examples for PING, SET/GET with varying payload sizes, LPUSH/LPOP and hash workloads. We will also examine the common causes of poor performance: network round-trip time, C P U-bound command cost, memory saturation and eviction policy, and the persistence options that produce spikes. Finally, you’ll get hands-on practice interpreting P99 and P99.9 latency values and learn safe tuning steps to try first. As you go through the chapter, think about which metric would matter most for your application: consistent low latency or maximum throughput?

screens.title: What is benchmarking? Key metrics
screens.narratorSegment: Benchmarking is the disciplined measurement of a system under repeatable conditions. For Redis, the two fundamental metrics are throughput — how many requests per second the system handles — and latency — how long each request takes to complete. Throughput and latency are related but distinct: you can have high throughput with poor tail latency if many requests complete quickly while a small fraction are slow. That’s why percentile metrics like P50, P99 and P99.9 are essential: they tell you the experience of typical requests and of the slowest requests that still affect users. A concrete example: a benchmark may report 100,000 requests per second for small GETs with an average latency of 0.5 milliseconds, but a P99 of 10 milliseconds. That P99 means one percent of requests experience a 20x slower response, which might break time-sensitive features. A common misconception is to treat average latency as the only signal; averages hide tail problems. Key takeaway: collect both RPS and percentile latency so you know whether your system is consistently fast or simply fast most of the time. What is benchmarking? Key metrics means measure both throughput and latency percentiles. tail latency reveals rare but harmful delays that averages can hide.. In practical terms, throughput, latency, and percentile thinking. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Benchmarking Basics
Key metrics defined
What to collect and why each metric matters
Throughput (RPS)
Operations per second; useful for capacity planning and comparing command types.
Latency (avg, P50, P99)
Average shows common case; percentiles reveal tail behavior important for user experience.
Latency distribution
Look for long tails that indicate occasional expensive operations or network spikes.
Example
A benchmark shows 120k RPS, avg latency 0.6ms, P99 12ms. The P99 points to operations that occasionally block or hit network issues and require further investigation.
Interpretation bullets
  • High RPS with high P99: many requests succeed quickly but some are slow — check blocking commands and persistence spikes.
  • Low RPS with low latency: possibly limited by client concurrency or network RTT.
  • Latency grows with value size: larger payloads increase network and serialization time.
Key Takeaway

Collect both RPS and percentile latency. Investigate tail latency before optimizing averages.

screens.title: Using redis-benchmark
screens.narratorSegment: Redis-benchmark is the practical tool you’ll use to generate repeatable workloads and capture throughput and latency. The core flags to know are -n for total requests, -c for concurrent clients, -t for the command list, -d for data size in bytes, and --latency-dist to print percentile distributions. Run a basic PING test to get a network- and command-cost baseline. Next, run SET/GET with varying -d sizes to compare the impact of payload size on RPS and latency. An important practice is to keep the command mix and request count constant while you change one variable at a time. For example, change -d from 10 to 1024 to 10240 and compare SET/GET numbers; you’ll often see RPS drop and latencies rise as payload increases. A common pitfall is benchmarking across a WAN: high RTT inflates latency and hides server processing capability. Use local or low-latency testbeds, or at least interpret results in the context of your network. Finally, capture the output and save it so you can compare experiments and revert changes if needed. Using redis-benchmark means change one flag at a time while keeping requests and command mixes constant to see true cause-and-effect.. In practical terms, flags, commands, and representative workloads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › redis-benchmark Usage
Common commands
Examples to run in your terminal
# Basic benchmark: 100,000 requests, 50 clients, PING
redis-benchmark -n 100000 -c 50 -t PING

# SET/GET with 1KB data size
redis-benchmark -n 100000 -c 100 -d 1024 -t SET,GET

# LPUSH/LPOP test
redis-benchmark -n 100000 -c 50 -t LPUSH,LPOP

# Latency distribution for SET
redis-benchmark -n 100000 -c 50 -t SET --latency-dist
Best practices
  • Run in a controlled environment with similar dataset size and network topology.
  • Vary one parameter at a time: concurrency, payload size, or command mix.
  • Use --latency-dist to capture tail percentiles such as P99 and P99.9.
  • Save outputs for comparison and document the exact command used.
Key Takeaway

Use representative workloads and consistent flags so you can trust comparisons between runs.

screens.title: Interpreting benchmark output
screens.narratorSegment: When you read redis-benchmark output, compare RPS and latency percentiles together to form an action plan. High RPS with low average latency but a spiky P99 suggests occasional blocking work or input and output spikes. For example, if SETs have 150k RPS and average 0.4ms but P99 is 15ms, look for persistence-related fsync spikes or occasional large commands. On the other hand, low RPS with low tail latency may indicate network RTT or insufficient client concurrency. If larger value sizes reduce RPS dramatically while C P U and memory remain low, the network and serialization cost are likely limiting factors. A common misconception is to change many configuration items at once; that yields ambiguous results. Instead, run a baseline, change one setting—like enabling pipelining or adjusting appendfsync—and re-run the same benchmark. Keep a short experiment log with the exact redis-benchmark command so you can reproduce and revert if necessary. Always validate changes in staging before production. Interpreting benchmark output means use both throughput and multiple latency percentiles to determine whether the server, network, or a specific command is the bottleneck.. In practical terms, requests per second vs latency percentiles and what they imply. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Interpreting Output
Typical result patterns
High RPS, high P99
Suggests occasional expensive ops: blocking commands, persistence fsync, or large object processing.
Low RPS, low P99
May be limited by client concurrency or network RTT rather than server processing.
RPS drops with larger payloads
Network bandwidth and serialization are likely bottlenecks.
Actionable checklist
  • Record baseline outputs and exact commands used.
  • Change one parameter and re-run the same workload.
  • If P99 rises, inspect SLOWLOG and persistence activity.
  • If RPS drops with larger payloads, test pipelining or collocating clients and server.
Common Mistake

Running benchmarks over a WAN without accounting for RTT can misattribute network-induced latency to server performance.

screens.title: Network latency and pipelining
screens.narratorSegment: Network round-trip time is often the invisible limiter of Redis throughput, especially for small commands. Redis processes commands in a single-threaded fashion, so each network RTT adds overhead even when the server is idle. A practical mitigation is pipelining: the client sends many commands without waiting for each reply, then reads the replies in batch. Pipelining reduces the number of RTTs and can dramatically increase effective throughput for many small operations. For example, a client that needs to write 1,000 keys can either send 1,000 individual SETs and wait for 1,000 responses, or pipeline groups of 100 SETs and reduce the number of RTT waits to 10. A misconception is that pipelining changes atomicity; pipelining only changes network behavior — it does not guarantee atomic multi-command semantics the way MULTI/EXEC does. When you test pipelining in redis-benchmark or in your client library, measure both RPS and tail latency to ensure pipelining benefits the overall latency profile. Consider also collocating client and server or using faster network interfaces to further lower RTT. Network latency and pipelining means group commands to lower the number of round-trips required; pipelining increases throughput without changing command semantics.. In practical terms, why rtt matters and how pipelining reduces its cost. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Network & Pipelining
Why RTT matters
Each request incurs a network round-trip. Reduce the number of round-trips to raise throughput.
Small commands are most sensitive to RTT because command processing time is tiny compared to network latency.
Collocating clients and Redis or using faster NICs reduces RTT and improves measurable performance.
Pipelining groups commands to reduce the total RTT count without changing server-side semantics.
Pipelining example
Client intent: set 1,000 keys
No pipelining
1,000 requests and 1,000 RTTs; higher overall latency due to many network trips.
With pipelining
Batch into 10 groups of 100: only 10 RTTs, dramatically increasing throughput.
Misconception

Pipelining does not provide atomicity. Use MULTI/EXEC when you need atomic multi-command semantics.

screens.title: CPU, persistence, and I/O effects
screens.narratorSegment: Redis is single-threaded for command execution, but it uses additional threads for background tasks such as input and output and persistence. C P U consumption becomes a bottleneck when commands themselves are expensive — heavy Lua scripts, large sorts, or commands with O(N) complexity on very large collections. Monitor used_cpu_sys and used_cpu_user from the INFO output to detect C P U pressure. Persistence also affects latency: RDB snapshots fork a child process and AOF uses fsync. An aggressive AOF policy like appendfsync always will produce consistent durability but can introduce frequent fsyncs that spike latency. RDB saving can cause pauses if data is very large during fork. Common mitigation strategies include switching appendfsync to everysec for a balance of durability and latency, scheduling snapshots outside peak hours, and offloading heavy processing to workers where possible. A misconception is blaming Redis for all latency spikes: sometimes long garbage collection or input and output on the host can be the real culprit. Always correlate Redis metrics with host-level C P U and disk activity when investigating. CPU, persistence, and I/O effects means expensive commands and persistence options create latency spikes; measure system cpu and i/o alongside redis metrics before changing configs.. In practical terms, how cpu-bound commands and persistence affect latency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › CPU & Persistence
CPU and command cost
Expensive commands can make Redis CPU-bound even with idle network.
Monitor used_cpu_sys and used_cpu_user to spot CPU pressure.
Profile or inspect slowlog for long-running commands and expensive Lua scripts.
Offload heavy computation or precompute values when feasible.
Persistence trade-offs
AOF and RDB provide durability but can introduce latency spikes.
appendfsync always gives strongest durability but highest latency from frequent fsyncs.
appendfsync everysec balances durability and latency; RDB snapshots fork and may stall on large datasets.
Test persistence settings under load to observe real latency impact.
Misconception

Changing persistence settings without measuring can improve one metric while degrading durability or causing unexpected latency elsewhere.

screens.title: Memory, maxmemory, and eviction
screens.narratorSegment: Redis stores data in memory, so memory usage is a first-class performance and safety concern. The maxmemory setting caps the amount of R A M Redis will use. When memory approaches this cap, Redis enforces the configured maxmemory-policy. Policies like allkeys-lru or volatile-lru evict keys based on least-recently-used heuristics and are useful for cache workloads. noeviction causes Redis to return errors for writes once memory is exhausted, which protects data at the cost of write availability. High memory fragmentation can waste R A M and push you closer to maxmemory than the raw dataset size suggests. A common mistake is setting maxmemory too close to system R A M without leaving headroom for OS and Redis overhead. Measure used_memory and monitor eviction stats and hit ratios. If you must preserve all data, prefer noeviction and provision sufficient R A M; if you use Redis as a cache, choose an eviction policy and validate its behavior under realistic access patterns. Always test eviction in staging so you understand which keys are evicted under load. Memory, maxmemory, and eviction means set maxmemory and choose an eviction policy aligned with whether redis is a cache or a primary store; leave headroom for the os.. In practical terms, how memory settings affect behavior and safety. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Memory & Eviction
maxmemory and policies
Choose a policy that matches your tolerance for data loss and write availability.
allkeys-lru: evict any key and prefer least-recently-used for caches.
volatile-lru: evict only keys with an expiration; useful when some keys are cacheable.
noeviction: stop writes when memory exhausted; preserves data at the cost of availability.
Practical guidance
  • Leave headroom for OS and Redis overhead; do not set maxmemory equal to total system RAM.
  • Monitor memory_fragmentation_ratio and used_memory_peak.
  • Simulate eviction in staging to verify that important keys are not dropped unexpectedly.

screens.title: Data structures and command complexity
screens.narratorSegment: Redis performance is heavily influenced by the data structures you choose and the commands you run against them. O(1) commands such as GET and SET are predictable and fast for single keys. In contrast, O(N) commands scale linearly with the number of elements they operate on; examples include LRANGE on a very long list, SMEMBERS on a huge set, or KEYS * which scans all keys. Using O(N) commands on large collections will show up in benchmarks as high P99 or P99.9 latency spikes and can block other operations. The recommended practice is to avoid blocking full-dataset commands in production and instead use the SCAN family (SCAN, HSCAN, SSCAN, ZSCAN) which iterates without blocking. Another technique is to model large sets as many smaller buckets so that per-operation cost stays small. A common misconception is that Redis can handle KEYS * at any scale; this is only safe for very small datasets or maintenance windows. When designing your data model, prefer operations that have known, stable complexity and test scale effects with redis-benchmark using realistic dataset sizes. Data structures and command complexity means choose data structures and commands with stable, known complexity and avoid full-dataset blocking commands in production.. In practical terms, o(1) vs o(n): picking the right operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Tuning strategies: configuration and modeling
screens.narratorSegment: When you have benchmark results and a suspected bottleneck, follow an ordered tuning process. First, reproduce the issue in staging with a representative dataset and the same access pattern. Second, change the lowest-risk setting that could fix the symptom and rerun the identical benchmark. Typical low-risk first steps include enabling pipelining in the client, adjusting appendfsync from always to everysec for lower fsync frequency, or increasing concurrency in the benchmark to test client limits. Medium-risk steps include changing maxmemory-policy or sharding large collections. High-risk changes such as removing persistence or altering fundamental data semantics should be last and validated carefully. Data modeling changes — using hashes instead of many individual keys, or splitting large lists into buckets — often yield high impact. Also remember to monitor SLOWLOG to find expensive commands you might refactor. Keep clear notes of the exact command and config difference for each experiment so you can attribute impact and revert if needed. Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Terminal Lab
Run these steps
1. Verify Redis is running locally and note server metrics with INFO.
2. Run PING benchmark to get a baseline. Record RPS and latency.
3. Run SET/GET with -d 10, -d 1024, -d 10240 and compare results.
4. Run LPUSH/LPOP and HSET/HGETALL scenarios to simulate different data structures.

Starter commands
echo "--- Benchmarking PING ---"

redis-benchmark -n 100000 -c 50 -t SET,GET -d 1024
redis-benchmark -n 100000 -c 50 -t SET,GET -d 10240

redis-benchmark -n 100000 -c 50 -t HSET,HGETALL -r 1000000

After each run, save the output to a file with the command and timestamp. Compare RPS and P99 to see which dimension changed most.

screens.title: Common mistakes and monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: Several common mistakes repeatedly lead teams into confusing benchmark results. First, running benchmarks over WAN links can misattribute network-induced delays to Redis — always account for RTT. Second, changing multiple parameters simultaneously makes it impossible to know which change caused improvement. Third, using KEYS * or other full-collection commands in production can cause latency spikes that affect all clients. Monitoring helps you catch these issues: check SLOWLOG to find long-running commands, and inspect INFO fields like used_memory, instantaneous_ops_per_sec, and the C P U metrics to correlate with benchmark anomalies. If you see persistent P99 spikes, search the slow log for matching timestamps and identify the command type. Also monitor persistence events such as AOF fsyncs and RDB saves — these often align with latency spikes. A practical habit is to add a short experiment log whenever you run benchmarks: the exact command, server config changes, and observed RPS and P99. That makes future troubleshooting much faster and reduces the chance of repeating mistakes. Common mistakes and monitoring means use slowlog and info metrics to correlate benchmark spikes with specific commands or persistence events, and avoid testing over wan without context.. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you’ll learn how to measure Redis performance in a systematic way and then use that data to tune the system for real workloads. Benchmarking is the controlled act of generating load and observing throughput and latency. We rely on redis-benchmark to simulate concurrent clients and command mixes so you can compare requests per second and latency percentiles. Performance tuning means choosing the right configuration, data structures, and deployment topology to address the bottlenecks you discover. You will see concrete redis-benchmark examples for PING, SET/GET with varying payload sizes, LPUSH/LPOP and hash workloads. We will also examine the common causes of poor performance: network round-trip time, C P U-bound command cost, memory saturation and eviction policy, and the persistence options that produce spikes. Finally, you’ll get hands-on practice interpreting P99 and P99.9 latency values and learn safe tuning steps to try first. As you go through the chapter, think about which metric would matter most for your application: consistent low latency or maximum throughput?

By the end of these screens you will be able to run redis-benchmark to collect meaningful throughput and latency numbers, interpret percentile values such as P99, and detect when network round-trip time or data size is limiting performance. You will identify C P U, memory, and persistence effects on Redis behavior and choose targeted configuration changes. You will also practice modelling data so that you avoid O(N) commands on very large collections, and learn when to use SCAN-family commands. Each objective pairs a skill with why it matters: measurable baselines let you prove an improvement and not just guess, and safe tuning—like pipelining or changing appendfsync—reduces risk to production. We will include examples and a short mnemonic to help you remember which metric guides which decision. Throughout, you'll be asked to compare before-and-after performance so you can see the impact of a single change. This makes your tuning work accountable and repeatable.

This second objectives screen focuses on applied skills you will practice. You will learn to choose the right redis-benchmark flags: total requests, concurrency, command set, and data size. You’ll practice reading the '--latency-dist' distribution to find P99 and P99.9 spikes, which point to occasional expensive operations. You will also build the habit of comparing the same workload with and without pipelining or different persistence settings, so you can attribute outcomes to a single change. Finally, you will form an action plan: measure in staging, apply the least risky change first, monitor production, and have a rollback plan. These steps reduce the chance of accidental data loss or performance regressions. The objective descriptions include small mnemonics and a verification milestone so you can mark when you have demonstrated the skill confidently.

Benchmarking is the disciplined measurement of a system under repeatable conditions. For Redis, the two fundamental metrics are throughput — how many requests per second the system handles — and latency — how long each request takes to complete. Throughput and latency are related but distinct: you can have high throughput with poor tail latency if many requests complete quickly while a small fraction are slow. That’s why percentile metrics like P50, P99 and P99.9 are essential: they tell you the experience of typical requests and of the slowest requests that still affect users. A concrete example: a benchmark may report 100,000 requests per second for small GETs with an average latency of 0.5 milliseconds, but a P99 of 10 milliseconds. That P99 means one percent of requests experience a 20x slower response, which might break time-sensitive features. A common misconception is to treat average latency as the only signal; averages hide tail problems. Key takeaway: collect both RPS and percentile latency so you know whether your system is consistently fast or simply fast most of the time. What is benchmarking? Key metrics means measure both throughput and latency percentiles. tail latency reveals rare but harmful delays that averages can hide.. In practical terms, throughput, latency, and percentile thinking. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Redis-benchmark is the practical tool you’ll use to generate repeatable workloads and capture throughput and latency. The core flags to know are -n for total requests, -c for concurrent clients, -t for the command list, -d for data size in bytes, and --latency-dist to print percentile distributions. Run a basic PING test to get a network- and command-cost baseline. Next, run SET/GET with varying -d sizes to compare the impact of payload size on RPS and latency. An important practice is to keep the command mix and request count constant while you change one variable at a time. For example, change -d from 10 to 1024 to 10240 and compare SET/GET numbers; you’ll often see RPS drop and latencies rise as payload increases. A common pitfall is benchmarking across a WAN: high RTT inflates latency and hides server processing capability. Use local or low-latency testbeds, or at least interpret results in the context of your network. Finally, capture the output and save it so you can compare experiments and revert changes if needed. Using redis-benchmark means change one flag at a time while keeping requests and command mixes constant to see true cause-and-effect.. In practical terms, flags, commands, and representative workloads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When you read redis-benchmark output, compare RPS and latency percentiles together to form an action plan. High RPS with low average latency but a spiky P99 suggests occasional blocking work or input and output spikes. For example, if SETs have 150k RPS and average 0.4ms but P99 is 15ms, look for persistence-related fsync spikes or occasional large commands. On the other hand, low RPS with low tail latency may indicate network RTT or insufficient client concurrency. If larger value sizes reduce RPS dramatically while C P U and memory remain low, the network and serialization cost are likely limiting factors. A common misconception is to change many configuration items at once; that yields ambiguous results. Instead, run a baseline, change one setting—like enabling pipelining or adjusting appendfsync—and re-run the same benchmark. Keep a short experiment log with the exact redis-benchmark command so you can reproduce and revert if necessary. Always validate changes in staging before production. Interpreting benchmark output means use both throughput and multiple latency percentiles to determine whether the server, network, or a specific command is the bottleneck.. In practical terms, requests per second vs latency percentiles and what they imply. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Network round-trip time is often the invisible limiter of Redis throughput, especially for small commands. Redis processes commands in a single-threaded fashion, so each network RTT adds overhead even when the server is idle. A practical mitigation is pipelining: the client sends many commands without waiting for each reply, then reads the replies in batch. Pipelining reduces the number of RTTs and can dramatically increase effective throughput for many small operations. For example, a client that needs to write 1,000 keys can either send 1,000 individual SETs and wait for 1,000 responses, or pipeline groups of 100 SETs and reduce the number of RTT waits to 10. A misconception is that pipelining changes atomicity; pipelining only changes network behavior — it does not guarantee atomic multi-command semantics the way MULTI/EXEC does. When you test pipelining in redis-benchmark or in your client library, measure both RPS and tail latency to ensure pipelining benefits the overall latency profile. Consider also collocating client and server or using faster network interfaces to further lower RTT. Network latency and pipelining means group commands to lower the number of round-trips required; pipelining increases throughput without changing command semantics.. In practical terms, why rtt matters and how pipelining reduces its cost. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Redis is single-threaded for command execution, but it uses additional threads for background tasks such as input and output and persistence. C P U consumption becomes a bottleneck when commands themselves are expensive — heavy Lua scripts, large sorts, or commands with O(N) complexity on very large collections. Monitor used_cpu_sys and used_cpu_user from the INFO output to detect C P U pressure. Persistence also affects latency: RDB snapshots fork a child process and AOF uses fsync. An aggressive AOF policy like appendfsync always will produce consistent durability but can introduce frequent fsyncs that spike latency. RDB saving can cause pauses if data is very large during fork. Common mitigation strategies include switching appendfsync to everysec for a balance of durability and latency, scheduling snapshots outside peak hours, and offloading heavy processing to workers where possible. A misconception is blaming Redis for all latency spikes: sometimes long garbage collection or input and output on the host can be the real culprit. Always correlate Redis metrics with host-level C P U and disk activity when investigating. CPU, persistence, and I/O effects means expensive commands and persistence options create latency spikes; measure system cpu and i/o alongside redis metrics before changing configs.. Redis stores data in memory, so memory usage is a first-class performance and safety concern. The maxmemory setting caps the amount of R A M Redis will use. When memory approaches this cap, Redis enforces the configured maxmemory-policy. Policies like allkeys-lru or volatile-lru evict keys based on least-recently-used heuristics and are useful for cache workloads. noeviction causes Redis to return errors for writes once memory is exhausted, which protects data at the cost of write availability. High memory fragmentation can waste R A M and push you closer to maxmemory than the raw dataset size suggests. A common mistake is setting maxmemory too close to system R A M without leaving headroom for OS and Redis overhead. Measure used_memory and monitor eviction stats and hit ratios. If you must preserve all data, prefer noeviction and provision sufficient R A M; if you use Redis as a cache, choose an eviction policy and validate its behavior under realistic access patterns. Always test eviction in staging so you understand which keys are evicted under load. Redis performance is heavily influenced by the data structures you choose and the commands you run against them. O(1) commands such as GET and SET are predictable and fast for single keys. In contrast, O(N) commands scale linearly with the number of elements they operate on; examples include LRANGE on a very long list, SMEMBERS on a huge set, or KEYS * which scans all keys. Using O(N) commands on large collections will show up in benchmarks as high P99 or P99.9 latency spikes and can block other operations. The recommended practice is to avoid blocking full-dataset commands in production and instead use the SCAN family (SCAN, HSCAN, SSCAN, ZSCAN) which iterates without blocking. Another technique is to model large sets as many smaller buckets so that per-operation cost stays small. A common misconception is that Redis can handle KEYS * at any scale; this is only safe for very small datasets or maintenance windows. When designing your data model, prefer operations that have known, stable complexity and test scale effects with redis-benchmark using realistic dataset sizes. When you have benchmark results and a suspected bottleneck, follow an ordered tuning process. First, reproduce the issue in staging with a representative dataset and the same access pattern. Second, change the lowest-risk setting that could fix the symptom and rerun the identical benchmark. Typical low-risk first steps include enabling pipelining in the client, adjusting appendfsync from always to everysec for lower fsync frequency, or increasing concurrency in the benchmark to test client limits. Medium-risk steps include changing maxmemory-policy or sharding large collections. High-risk changes such as removing persistence or altering fundamental data semantics should be last and validated carefully. Data modeling changes — using hashes instead of many individual keys, or splitting large lists into buckets — often yield high impact. Also remember to monitor SLOWLOG to find expensive commands you might refactor. Keep clear notes of the exact command and config difference for each experiment so you can attribute impact and revert if needed. Several common mistakes repeatedly lead teams into confusing benchmark results. First, running benchmarks over WAN links can misattribute network-induced delays to Redis — always account for RTT. Second, changing multiple parameters simultaneously makes it impossible to know which change caused improvement. Third, using KEYS * or other full-collection commands in production can cause latency spikes that affect all clients. Monitoring helps you catch these issues: check SLOWLOG to find long-running commands, and inspect INFO fields like used_memory, instantaneous_ops_per_sec, and the C P U metrics to correlate with benchmark anomalies. If you see persistent P99 spikes, search the slow log for matching timestamps and identify the command type. These concept cards summarize the core ideas you should retain. First, redis-benchmark is the canonical utility to measure throughput and latency under controlled conditions. Use it to simulate concurrent clients and to record RPS and percentile latencies. Second, throughput and latency are complementary metrics: measure both and pay attention to tail percentiles like P99 and P99.9 because they reveal rare but impactful delays. Third, pipelining reduces network round-trips and often delivers large gains for many small operations — but it does not change atomicity.
